nodes.title: Role-based access control: Key Ideas
nodes.content: RBAC assigns permissions to roles, then users to roles — a layer of indirection that scales. Azure's RBAC, AWS's IAM, Kubernetes RBAC, and GCP's IAM all share the same mental model. Mastering one transfers directly to the others.

flashcards.front: Why use roles instead of granting permissions to users directly?
flashcards.back: Roles separate WHO from WHAT. Add a person to a role, they inherit the permissions. Remove them, they lose access instantly. Auditing: 'who can read prod?' becomes 'who's in the prod-readers role?' instead of scanning thousands of user-level policies. Onboarding/offboarding becomes role membership changes, not 500 permission grants.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between a built-in role and a custom role?
flashcards.back: Built-in: cloud-provided, covers common patterns (Owner, Contributor, Reader, Storage Admin). Can't be modified. Custom: you define the exact actions allowed — pick when built-ins are too broad or too narrow. Cost of custom roles: maintenance — every new service adds actions you may need to add.

flashcards.front: Scope — why is it as important as the role?
flashcards.back: Same role at different scopes = wildly different power. 'Contributor' at the subscription scope = god mode on the whole subscription. 'Contributor' on one resource group = limited to that group's resources. Always scope at the smallest unit that's practical — never grant subscription-level if resource-group-level works.

flashcards.front: RBAC vs ABAC — when do you need attributes?
flashcards.back: RBAC: permissions tied to fixed roles. Works great until you need rules like 'engineers can read their own team's resources but not others'. ABAC (attribute-based) evaluates request attributes (user.team, resource.team) at runtime. Most clouds support both — start with RBAC, add ABAC tags when the role explosion becomes painful.

nodes.title: Part 2: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 2. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: You want a container to use the `RuntimeDefault` seccomp profile to restrict its allowed syscalls. Which Pod spec achieves this in Kubernetes 1.27+?
flashcards.back: The correct modern approach (Kubernetes 1.22+) is to set `securityContext.seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault` in the container or Pod spec. This applies whatever the container runtime defines as its default seccomp filter. The annotation-based method (`seccomp.security.alpha.kubernetes.io`) is the legacy approach (deprecated). `Unconfined` explicitly disables seccomp filtering — the opposite of what is needed. There is no SeccompProfile CRD in standard Kubernetes.

flashcards.front: A security engineer is hardening worker nodes against the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark. They want the set of actions that aligns with the benchmark's node-level recommendations covering kubelet flags, file permissions on kubeconfig and PKI, and disabling read-only ports. Which set of actions fits?
flashcards.back: CIS benchmarks recommend minimizing the OS footprint: uninstall packages not needed for Kubernetes, disable or unload unnecessary kernel modules (`dccp`, `sctp`, `rds`, etc.), ensure only required services are running, and keep the system patched. Installing all packages increases the attack surface. Enabling all kernel modules provides more exploitation vectors. Running services as root violates the principle of least privilege.

flashcards.front: You need to permanently prevent the `dccp` kernel module from loading on a Kubernetes node. Which configuration achieves persistent blacklisting?
flashcards.back: To persistently blacklist a kernel module, add `blacklist dccp` to a file in `/etc/modprobe.d/` such as `/etc/modprobe.d/kubernetes-blacklist.conf`. You can also add `install dccp /bin/false` to prevent loading even when explicitly requested. A reboot applies the change. `modprobe -r` only unloads for the current session. `/etc/modules` lists modules to LOAD at boot, not blacklist. `systemctl` manages services, not kernel modules.

flashcards.front: A container escapes and needs root on the host. Which kernel feature in Kubernetes 1.30+, when enabled, limits the blast radius by mapping container UID 0 to an unprivileged host UID?
flashcards.back: User namespaces (`hostUsers: false` in the Pod spec, Kubernetes 1.30 stable) remap the container's root UID (0) to a high non-root host UID (100000+). If a container escapes, the process has no special privileges on the host — it's an unprivileged user. Seccomp and AppArmor reduce the attack surface but don't prevent host-level privileges if root escapes. `runAsNonRoot` prevents root inside the container but doesn't change the host UID mapping.

nodes.title: Incident response: Key Ideas
nodes.content: IR follows a documented lifecycle so a panicked 3am pager doesn't turn into 'what do we do now?'. The classic NIST flow is preparation, detection, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned. Exam questions test which phase owns which action.

flashcards.front: NIST IR lifecycle — name the phases.
flashcards.back: (1) Preparation: playbooks, contact lists, hardened images. (2) Detection & Analysis: SIEM alerts, IDS, user reports. (3) Containment: short-term (isolate host) + long-term (block C2 domains). (4) Eradication: remove malware, close vuln. (5) Recovery: restore from clean backup, monitor for re-infection. (6) Lessons learned: post-mortem within 2 weeks, action items tracked.

Short-term: stop the bleed fast — pull the network cable, kill the user session, block the IP. May be reversible. Long-term: durable fix — patch the vuln, rotate creds, deploy IPS rule, sometimes rebuild from scratch. Don't skip short-term: every minute of attacker dwell time multiplies damage.

flashcards.front: Chain of custody — why does it matter?
flashcards.back: If the incident leads to prosecution, evidence must be admissible — every transfer, image, and access logged from acquisition to court. Drives required to be hashed (SHA-256) immediately, copies (not originals) used for analysis, originals stored in a tamper-evident bag with signatures. Skip this and the lawyer dismisses your case.

flashcards.front: What's a post-mortem (lessons learned) supposed to produce?
flashcards.back: Blameless write-up within 2 weeks: timeline, what worked, what didn't, action items with owners + due dates. The goal is process improvement, not punishment — if engineers fear blame they hide details and the next incident is worse. Track action items in your normal sprint board, not in a doc nobody reopens.

nodes.title: Observability and monitoring: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Observability is metrics + logs + traces — the three pillars. You need all three to debug a production incident: metrics tell you something is wrong, logs tell you what happened, traces tell you where in the call graph the problem lives.

flashcards.front: Metrics vs logs vs traces — what does each tell you?
flashcards.back: Metrics: numeric time-series, cheap to store, perfect for dashboards and alerts ('p99 latency = 800 ms'). Logs: discrete events with context, expensive at scale, perfect for forensics. Traces: causally-linked spans showing a request's full path through services.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between an alert and a notification?
flashcards.back: An alert is a condition that fires when a metric crosses a threshold (CPU > 80% for 5 min). The notification is the resulting message (email, Slack, PagerDuty page). One alert can fan out to many notifications. Tuning alerts is harder than wiring notifications.

flashcards.front: What is an SLI / SLO / SLA?
flashcards.back: SLI (indicator): the metric you actually measure ('% of requests under 200 ms'). SLO (objective): the internal target ('99.9% of requests under 200 ms over 28 days'). SLA (agreement): the contractual promise to customers, usually weaker than the SLO so you have buffer.

Plain-text logs are unparseable at scale. Structured logs (JSON, with timestamp + level + service + request_id + key fields) are indexable, queryable, and join-able across services. Most platforms auto-extract fields from JSON without configuration.
